body_html:
The most common insurance disputes during peak weather in Dallas involve hail damage severity, wind damage versus wear and tear, low repair or replacement pricing, water intrusion and secondary damage, and denials blamed on pre-existing damage. Most of these are disagreements over the amount of loss, which a professional appraisal can often resolve.

North Texas does not ease into storm season. Spring brings large hail and supercells, summer adds straight-line winds and microbursts, and fall and winter can deliver more wind events and freezes. When thousands of Dallas-area claims hit carriers at once, disputes follow. This guide covers the five disputes we see most often, why storm-season claims get more pushback and how homeowners and property owners can respond.

Why does Dallas weather create so many insurance disputes?

Dallas-Fort Worth sits in one of the most hail-prone regions in the United States. The busiest stretch typically runs from March through June, with additional severe weather possible through the summer and fall. Our article on when peak weather season is in Dallas covers the calendar in more detail.

Large storms can affect entire neighborhoods across Dallas, Plano, Frisco, McKinney, Arlington and Fort Worth in a single afternoon. Carriers respond by bringing in catastrophe adjusters from across the country, who may be inspecting many roofs a day under pressure. That volume is the backdrop for nearly every dispute below.

What are the five most common insurance disputes during peak weather?

DisputeCarrier's typical positionEvidence that helps the policyholder
Hail damage severityDamage is minor or cosmetic; repair a few shinglesSlope-by-slope test squares, soft-metal dents, hail size reports
Wind damage vs. wear and tearMissing shingles are due to age or installationStorm wind reports, creased and unsealed shingles, directional patterns
Undervalued repair costsEstimate pricing is correct for the areaLine-item estimate with local pricing and complete scope
Water intrusion and secondary damageLeak is a maintenance issue or long-term seepageDate-stamped photos, moisture readings, link to storm opening
Pre-existing damageDamage came from an earlier stormPrior inspections, photos, purchase records, storm date data

1. Disagreements over hail damage severity

This is the most frequent Dallas storm dispute. The adjuster sees a few hits and approves a small repair; your roofer sees bruising on every slope and recommends replacement. The disagreement often comes down to inspection thoroughness and whether impacts fractured the shingle mat or were merely cosmetic. Read insurance appraisal for hail damage claims for how these disputes are typically resolved.

2. Conflicts over wind damage versus wear and tear

When shingles go missing after a windstorm, carriers sometimes argue the roof was already failing because of age, poor nailing or broken seal strips from heat. Wind-lifted shingles may also settle back down, hiding broken seals. A careful inspection that checks seals and documents directional patterns consistent with the storm is the best response.

3. Undervaluation of repair or replacement costs

Even when the carrier accepts storm damage, the estimate may leave out line items or use pricing that does not reflect post-storm demand for labor and materials in the Dallas market. Missing flashing, vents, drip edge, steep charges and code items are common. Our guide to why insurance companies underscope roof damage lists the usual gaps.

4. Disputes over water intrusion and secondary damage

Storm openings let water into attics, ceilings and walls. Carriers sometimes characterize those leaks as long-term seepage or a maintenance problem, which many policies exclude. Prompt photos, moisture readings and evidence tying the leak to a storm-created opening are critical. Act fast to dry the area and prevent mold, and keep receipts for mitigation.

5. Claim denials due to alleged pre-existing damage

With multiple storms a year in North Texas, carriers may argue that damage happened during an earlier event, especially if you did not file a claim at the time. Prior inspection reports, real estate inspection photos, dated pictures of the roof and storm data for your specific date of loss help separate one event from another.

Tip: Take a quick set of roof and exterior photos each spring before storm season. Dated "before" photos are one of the simplest ways to defeat a pre-existing damage argument later.

Why do storm-season claims face more pushback?

  • Volume: adjusters handle more claims with less time per inspection.
  • Unfamiliar adjusters: out-of-state catastrophe adjusters may not know North Texas building practices or pricing.
  • Desk review: some claims are scoped from photos or aerial reports with limited field verification.
  • Deductibles: percentage wind/hail deductibles mean small estimates may produce no payment, which frustrates homeowners and invites disputes. See why peak season matters to your insurance deductible in Dallas.
  • Multiple events: back-to-back storms make causation and date-of-loss questions harder.

What Texas rules apply to Dallas storm claims?

Texas Insurance Code Chapter 542 sets prompt payment deadlines. Generally, a carrier must acknowledge your claim within 15 days, accept or reject it within 15 business days of receiving the information it requested (with extensions possible up to 45 days), and pay within 5 business days after accepting it. Catastrophe declarations can extend some of these deadlines, so check with your carrier and track dates with our Texas claim deadline calculator.

For weather-related claims, Chapter 542A generally requires 61 days' written notice before filing a lawsuit. And most Texas homeowners and commercial policies include an appraisal clause that either party can invoke when the dispute is about the amount of loss. You can read the statutes at statutes.capitol.texas.gov. This is general information, not legal advice.

How do professional appraisals resolve these disputes?

A structured, evidence-based process

In appraisal, each side appoints its own appraiser. The two appraisers inspect, exchange estimates and try to agree. If they cannot, a neutral umpire resolves the remaining items, and an award signed by any two of the three generally sets the amount of loss.

Detailed reports and industry-standard pricing

A strong appraisal presentation includes slope-by-slope documentation, interior damage records, and a line-item estimate in Xactimate or Symbility, the same platforms carriers use. Speaking the carrier's language makes differences easy to identify and resolve. Where interior damage is involved, Matterport 3D documentation captures conditions before repairs begin, so every party reviews the same evidence.

Appraisal versus litigation

Appraisal is usually faster and less expensive than a lawsuit, and it focuses only on the amount of loss. Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), appraisers can assess the extent and cause of damage but do not decide coverage. That makes appraisal well suited to severity, pricing and scope disputes, and less suited to outright coverage denials.

What to expect once appraisal is invoked

  1. One party sends a written appraisal demand under the policy's appraisal clause.
  2. Each side names a competent, disinterested appraiser, usually within a period the policy sets (often 20 days).
  3. The appraisers inspect the property, review documentation and exchange estimates.
  4. If they agree, they sign an award. If not, they select or request an umpire to decide the items still in dispute.
  5. The carrier reviews the award and issues payment under the policy terms, less the deductible and prior payments.

Timelines vary with the size of the loss and how quickly each side responds. Our insurance appraisal timeline guide walks through each stage.

Do Dallas commercial and multifamily owners face the same disputes?

Yes, and the dollar amounts are usually larger. Apartment complexes, retail centers, office buildings and warehouses across the Metroplex face the same five disputes, often multiplied across many buildings and roof sections. A single hailstorm can damage dozens of multifamily roofs, HVAC units and windows at one property.

Commercial claims add complications: percentage wind/hail deductibles that apply per building or per occurrence, tenant leases that assign repair responsibilities, business income questions and engineers hired by the carrier. Low-slope roofs can also hide wet insulation that changes the scope from patching to replacement. The same principles apply, though: thorough documentation, a complete line-item estimate and, when needed, appraisal to settle the amount of loss.

What do these disputes look like in practice?

The scenarios below are illustrative examples, not actual client cases.

  • Hail scope gap: a carrier approves repairs to two slopes of a Plano home, while the homeowner's roofer documents functional hail damage on all six. Appraisal focuses the panel on test-square evidence for each slope.
  • Wind versus wear: after a summer microburst in Arlington, a carrier attributes missing shingles to age. Photos of creased, unsealed shingles on the windward side and local wind reports support storm causation.
  • Water intrusion: a Dallas homeowner finds a ceiling stain days after a storm, and the carrier calls it a maintenance leak. Moisture readings, dated photos and a documented storm opening above the stain tie the damage to the event.

Tips for filing claims during Dallas peak weather season

  1. Photograph your roof and exterior before storm season and again right after each storm.
  2. Report damage promptly in writing and record your claim number and adjuster's contact information.
  3. Mitigate further damage with tarps or water extraction and keep receipts.
  4. Have your own roofer present during the adjuster inspection.
  5. Ask for the carrier's full estimate and photos, and compare them line by line.
  6. Keep a single folder, paper or digital, with every estimate, photo, receipt and letter.

Next steps: when to bring in a professional appraiser

Consider appraisal when the carrier agrees the damage is covered but the gap between estimates is significant, reinspections have not closed it, and you have solid documentation. faqs.q: When is hail season in Dallas?
faqs.a: Hail risk in Dallas-Fort Worth is highest in spring, generally from March through June, when strong storms and supercells are most common. Severe storms with hail and damaging wind can still occur in summer and fall, so it is smart to document your roof before spring and check it after any significant storm.

faqs.q: What should I do if my Dallas hail claim is underpaid?
faqs.a: Request the carrier's full estimate and photos, then have a roofer prepare a line-item comparison showing missing or short items. Submit that evidence and ask for a reinspection in writing. If the gap remains and the carrier accepts the damage is covered, appraisal under your policy may be the most efficient way to resolve it.

faqs.q: Can my insurance company blame storm damage on an old roof?
faqs.a: Carriers sometimes attribute damage to age, wear or poor installation. That position can be challenged with evidence such as creased or unsealed shingles, directional damage patterns, collateral damage to soft metals and weather data for your date of loss. Prior photos or inspections showing the roof's condition before the storm are especially helpful.

faqs.q: Do Texas prompt payment deadlines apply after a big storm?
faqs.a: Yes, Chapter 542 still applies, but carriers may get additional time when a weather-related catastrophe is declared. Generally, insurers must acknowledge claims within 15 days and decide within 15 business days of receiving requested information. Track your dates carefully and ask the carrier in writing if it claims an extension.

faqs.q: Is appraisal better than suing my insurance company?
faqs.a: Appraisal is usually faster and less expensive than litigation, and it works well when the only dispute is the amount of loss. It does not resolve coverage denials or bad-faith claims. Many property owners use appraisal first and consult an attorney only if coverage or conduct issues remain after the award.
